title: The Knock — A Scholarship Arrives
subtitle: Sen: what can he actually do and be?

lines.text: A scholarship announcement — tuition covered, study expenses assisted. He is eligible.
Aarav. You should apply.
No.
You haven't even read it.
I have work here.
But you wanted this.
That was years ago. I changed.
Or did the choices available to you change first?
You think you understand my life because you remember what I wanted at seventeen?
I'm not deciding for you. I'm asking.
Then ask without already knowing the answer.
Later that evening — a different conversation.
Do you want to apply?
I don't know.
Would you go if the money were enough?
Maybe. But then who helps here? What if I fail? Everyone will say I wasted the chance.
Those are real worries.
I'm not afraid of studying. I'm tired of building my life around a possibility that might not work.
Then maybe the question is not whether you want to study. It is whether studying can be made possible without everything else collapsing.
His mother has reframed the problem. Not "What do you desire?" but "What can actually be made available to you?"
Amartya Sen, in On Ethics and Economics, argues that evaluating a person's well-being only through their satisfaction — through utility — gives us an incomplete picture.
A person can be content and still lack freedoms that matter. Happiness is real evidence, but it is not the whole of a life.
Sen asks us to look at the opportunities and real freedoms available to a person, not only at what they report feeling.
Aarav's satisfaction is not fake. His skill and family contribution are genuine. But so is the question of whether he has a meaningful chance to pursue education if he decides he wants it.

shots.card:
Is he satisfied?
—
What can he actually do and be?

lines.text: The utilitarian asks: Is he satisfied? Sen asks: What can he actually do and be?
